---
title: Agent
description: Agent = ReAct. The loop primitive that thinks, acts (tool call), observes the result, and repeats until done.
---

> A user asks *"what's the weather in Paris?"*. Your code can't just hit a weather API — the LLM has to decide which tool to call, with what args, then read the result, then decide whether to call another tool or respond. **That decide → act → observe → repeat is what makes an Agent an Agent**, not a function call.

## Agent = ReAct

The Agent primitive **is** the ReAct loop (Yao 2022). One iteration:

```
LLM call → route → [tool calls → loop] OR [final answer]
```

Each iteration: the LLM produces text + optional tool calls. If tools were called, the framework executes them, appends results to the message history, and starts another iteration. If no tools were called (or `maxIterations` is hit), the loop exits with the final text.

**If it doesn't loop-with-tools, it isn't an Agent — it's an [LLMCall](doc:key-concepts#1-llmcall--one-call).**

## Build an agent

`Agent.create({ provider, model })` → builder. `.system(...)` sets the system prompt. `.tool(...)` registers tools (each with a JSON schema). `.build()` finalizes:

<CodeFile path="examples/core/02-agent-with-tools.ts" region="build" title="examples/core/02-agent-with-tools.ts (region: build)" />

The framework owns the iteration loop. You declare what tools the agent has; the LLM decides when (and with what args) to call them; the framework dispatches and feeds results back.

## What `run()` takes

A message, in either spelling:

```ts
await agent.run('what is the weather in Paris?');            // a bare string IS the message
await agent.run({ message: 'what is the weather in Paris?' }); // identical, byte for byte
await agent.run({ message: '…', identity: { tenant: 'globex', conversationId: 'c2' } });
```

Anything that is not a message is refused **before the run starts**, with an `InvalidRunInputError` naming the door and what arrived — `{}`, `{ message: 42 }`, `null`, and an empty or whitespace-only message. Nothing is billed and no half-run has to be explained.

An empty message is refused rather than sent: it is not a shorter question, it reaches a provider as a turn with no content, and real wires reject it. To run on the system prompt alone, say so in the message (`run({ message: 'begin' })`).

The same rule holds for `LLMCall`, `Sequence`, `Parallel`, `Conditional` and `Loop` — one door, one answer.

## Observe the loop

Because the framework owns the loop, observability is just attaching listeners — no SDK, no agent-instrumentation wrapper:

<CodeFile path="examples/core/02-agent-with-tools.ts" region="observe" title="examples/core/02-agent-with-tools.ts (region: observe)" />

118 typed events fire across 26 domains during a single `agent.run()`. See the [Observability guide](doc:observability) for the full taxonomy.

## maxIterations

Every Agent has a `maxIterations` cap (default 10). The loop exits when:

1. The LLM returns text with no tool calls (normal completion)
2. `maxIterations` is reached (forced exit — see *Running out of budget* below)
3. A tool throws (propagates as an error; subject to `withRetry` if wrapped)
4. The agent pauses via `askHuman` / `pauseHere` (`run()` returns a `RunnerPauseOutcome` instead of a string — narrow it with the `isPaused()` guard)

Tune `maxIterations` to your tool budget. Tool-heavy agents (research, code-gen) commonly run 15–30; chat agents 3–5.

### Running out of budget

`maxIterations` is a cap on **actions**, and the model does not know it is about to be hit.
Through 9.55.0, a turn that reached the cap while the model was still asking for tools handed
back whatever text happened to ride that last call. Mid-task, that is a fragment:

> "The third finding focus is not settling… Let me check what's on screen now:"

That sentence reached the person as if it were the answer, with nothing on the record saying the
budget had run out.

**Since 9.56.0 the run spends one more LLM call with the tools withheld**, carrying one
instruction, and hands back what comes back:

> [budget exhausted — the action budget was exhausted before the wrap-up call this message
> opened, so no tools were offered on that call. That call was for the final answer, from what
> the messages above already hold: what was completed, what remained undone, and anything the
> person should know.]

The bracketed opening is not decoration: it is the marker that tells the window's refusal engine
and a routing rule reading `history` that the library wrote this message, not the person (see
`isSaidByPerson`). And every clause reports the call it was written for in the past tense,
because the message stays in `history` and is re-read on every later call of the turn.

That call is exempt from `maxIterations` by construction, not by exception: a model offered no
tools has nothing to ask for, so it can only answer. It costs one call, and it is on the record
like any other turn — its own `iteration_start`, `llm_start` and `cost.tick`.

The fact is on the record three ways — `agent.stoppedEarly()`,
`agentfootprint.agent.budget_exhausted`, and a `stoppedEarly` field on
`agentfootprint.agent.turn_end` — so a dashboard can tell *answered* from *answered after the
budget ran out*:

```ts
const answer = await agent.run({ message: 'Audit the three findings' });

agent.stoppedEarly();
// { reason: 'max-iterations', iteration: 8, pendingToolCalls: 1,
//   answerWasEmpty: false, wrappedUp: true }

agent.on('agentfootprint.agent.budget_exhausted', (e) => e.payload);
// { reason: 'max-iterations', iteration: 8, limit: 8,
//   pendingToolCalls: 1, action: 'wrapped-up' }

agent.on('agentfootprint.agent.turn_end', (e) => e.payload.stoppedEarly);
// { reason: 'max-iterations', iteration: 8, pendingToolCalls: 1, wrappedUp: true }
```

It rides the **iteration** budget only. A halting `costBudget` keeps the old behaviour, because
there you capped the money and one more call would spend past the cap — an action cap says
nothing about a call that takes no action.

Turn it off with `wrapUpAtMaxIterations: false` (the fact is still recorded, as
`action: 'cut-short'`). A turn that never runs out of budget is byte-identical either way —
same calls, same events, same committed state.

<CodeFile path="examples/features/67-out-of-budget-wrap-up.ts" region="wrap-up" title="examples/features/67-out-of-budget-wrap-up.ts (region: wrap-up)" />

## Identity for multi-tenant memory

If your agent uses memory (`.memory(...)`), every `.run()` call must include an `identity` so memory is scoped per tenant / principal / conversation:

```ts
await agent.run({
  message: 'How long do refunds take?',
  identity: { tenant: 'acme', principal: 'alice', conversationId: 'thread-42' },
});
```

Without an identity, memory falls back to a global namespace — fine for single-user prototypes, dangerous in production multi-tenant apps. See [Memory guide](doc:memory).

## Per-run config — `.configure()`

An agent is built once and run many times, but not every run wants the same model
or the same house rules. A long message may deserve the bigger model; a tenant may
have its own policy text; a canary may want last week's prompt.

Rebuilding the whole agent per request works and is wasteful. Reaching in and
mutating one is worse — the trace then describes an agent that no longer exists.

`.configure((ctx) => ({ model?, instructions? }))` resolves **once per run**, at
the start of the run:

<CodeFile path="examples/features/36-per-run-config.ts" region="configure" title="examples/features/36-per-run-config.ts (region: configure)" />

`ctx` is a `RunConfigContext`: the run's `message`, its `identity` (when
`run({ identity })` supplied one), its `runId`, and `defaults` — what the agent
was **built** with, so a resolver can decide relative to it rather than restating
it. The return value is a `RunConfig`; the resolver's own type is `RunConfigFn`.

### Typing a resolver that lives somewhere else

The inline form above needs no annotations — TypeScript infers `ctx` from
`.configure()`. A resolver you keep in its own module does need them, so
`RunConfigFn`, `RunConfigContext` and `RunConfig` are all exported from
`agentfootprint`. Import them rather than re-declaring the shape by hand: a
hand copy stops matching the moment the context grows a field, and it stops
matching silently.

```ts
import type { RunConfig, RunConfigContext, RunConfigFn } from 'agentfootprint';

// A named resolver, testable on its own and shared across agents.
export const pickBrain: RunConfigFn = (ctx) =>
  ctx.message.length > 500 ? { model: 'big-model' } : {};

// A factory naming its own return type.
export function houseRulesFor(tenant: string) {
  return (ctx: RunConfigContext): RunConfig => ({
    instructions: `${ctx.defaults.instructions}\n\n${rulesFor(tenant)}`,
  });
}

const agent = Agent.create({ provider, model: 'small-model' })
  .system('You answer support questions.')
  .configure(pickBrain)
  .build();
```

### What gets resolved gets committed

This is the part that matters. A run that changed its own model without recording
it would be a trace that lies about its most expensive fact — you would read the
recording, see the model the agent was constructed with, and be wrong about which
one answered.

So the resolved values ride the same commit that already carries the run's other
run-level facts (identity, iteration budget, turn number): `resolvedModel` and
`resolvedInstructions` land in the commit log **before the first LLM call**, and
the LLM call reads them from there. One value, used and recorded:

```ts
await agent.run({ message, identity: { tenant: 'globex', conversationId: 'c2' } });

const state = agent.getLastSnapshot()?.sharedState;
state.resolvedModel;        // 'big-model'  — what actually answered
state.resolvedInstructions; // the rules that run actually ran under
```

The `agentfootprint.stream.llm_start` event reports the resolved model too, and
cost is priced against it — there is no second copy to drift.

### Absent means unchanged

Omit `.configure()` and every run behaves, and records, exactly as it did before:
no extra scope writes, no extra scope reads, and the request bytes are identical.
The same is true of a resolver that returns `{}` or nothing — only what it
actually returned is committed, so "I looked and decided not to change anything"
costs nothing in the log.

### This is the run axis only

Tools are the *iteration* axis and already have an owner: `.toolProvider()`,
consulted every iteration so gates can react to what just happened. `.configure()`
deliberately does not duplicate it, and does not reach past `model` and
`instructions` into the rest of the run — `temperature`, `maxTokens` and the tool
set stay where they were set.

Calling `.configure()` twice throws. A silently-overridden resolver is a config
that lies.

## Findings on the record — `.findings()`

Call `.findings()` on the builder and every served tool schema gains one reserved, optional argument, `_findings` (the constant `RESERVED_ARGUMENT`). On each tool call the model declares why it is calling — a `Basis` of `direct` or `exploratory`, with an optional `Expect` bucket of `low`, `medium` or `high` — and, on its next tool call or as a top-level key of a JSON answer, the `Standing` of each earlier tool result: `fact`, `open`, `noise` or `ruled-out`. The wire shape of that declaration is `FindingsDeclaration`.

The library peels the argument off before the tool, the permission gate, middleware or any argument validation sees it, and appends what was declared to one state key, `findingsLedger`, typed `FindingsLedger`: a list of `FindingsRow` entries, where a `BasisRow` records a declared call, a `StandingRow` records a declared standing together with the assertions the model stands on, and a `ConflictRow` names, by `ConflictWitness` identities only, two standing facts that disagree. Nothing is inferred: a call that carries no declaration writes no row, and a result the model never names is undeclared — never `open`. Read the ledger back with `agent.findings()`.

```ts
const agent = Agent.create({ provider, model }).tool(search).tool(fetchPage).findings().build();
await agent.run({ message: 'Which region is the outage in?' });
agent.findings(); // basis, standing and conflict rows, in the order they were declared
```

There are no extra model calls, and an agent that never calls `.findings()` records exactly the bytes it recorded before.

### Naming a result — the offer

On a hosted model the ask "by its tool_result id" produced standings named by ordinal — `"0"`, `"1"` — which the ledger records honestly as `unknownId` and which settle nothing: a model does not copy a long opaque id out of prose, it counts. So from the second call on, the reserved `_findings` property on every served schema lists, in `previous[].toolCallId`, the ids the model may name — an `enum` of the tool results on the wire the model can still read, newest first, at most 32, and a clipped list says so in the property's description. A result with no standing, a `fact` and an `open` result stay listed, so a later call can revise a standing (`open` to `fact` once something settles it, `fact` to `ruled-out` when a conflict resolves — the ledger keeps the last standing per result); a result declared `noise` or `ruled-out` leaves the list, because it is a ticket on the wire and there is nothing left to re-judge. A result the window evicted is not on it, and the first call, with nothing to name, serves the base property unchanged. The offer is computed where the served history and the ledger meet, bound into the schema at the one decoration site and committed with the tool list, so `servedAt(snapshot, k).tools.schemas` carries exactly what was offered at call `k` and the receipt's schema hash moves when the offer does. What the model may copy is not what the library resolves: an id outside the offer is still filed as written, with `unknownId: true`, never mapped to a position or a tool name — and every id inside the offer resolves, because a standing is identified against the same served history the offer was read from, whichever call produced the result. A JSON answer has no schema to bind, so the instruction asks for the id exactly as the schema listed it, and standings declared there are counted apart.

Two things this costs. `.findings()` needs the tools slot rebuilt every call, so it is refused at build under `reactMode: 'classic'`, which caches that slot after the first turn; use the default `dynamic` mode or `dynamic-grouped`. And because the enum moves with the run, an armed agent's tool schemas differ from call to call, so a prompt-cache breakpoint placed on the tools block cannot hit on such a run and the breakpoints after it miss with it; no number for that trade has been measured, and the design page names the alternative not taken.

```json
{ "type": "string", "enum": ["toolu_01X…", "toolu_01W…"],
  "description": "The tool_result id being judged — one of the ids listed; a result not listed cannot be named here." }
```

### What the call set out to test — `proposition` and `predicts`

A `FindingsDeclaration` may carry two optional one-line strings on the call itself, written before its result exists: `proposition`, what the call tests (the schema recommends it when `basis` is `exploratory`), and `predicts`, what the result should show if the proposition holds. Both land on the `BasisRow`, each cut at 240 characters with the cut stated in the text; the `agentfootprint.findings.declared` event carries `hasProposition: true` and never the text. On the served piece an `open` or `ruled-out` line quotes the judged call's own proposition after the model's words, so what was ruled out reads against what the model set out to test rather than against hindsight; a fact line does not repeat it, and `predicts` is record-only. Nothing is inferred: no proposition declared, no `tested:` on the line.

```ts
// The model's third call, as sent: a basis with a proposition, and the previous result's standing.
{ name: 'search_logs', args: { q: 'fc1/7', _findings: {
    basis: 'exploratory',
    proposition: 'the optic was swapped during the maintenance window',
    predicts: 'a swap entry for fc1/7 in the change log',
    previous: [{ toolCallId: 'toolu_01W…', standing: 'fact', assertions: [/* … */] }],
} } }
// …and the line the answer turn is later served, once the model rules it out:
// ruled out (search_logs, tool:toolu_01X…): no swap entry this week — tested: the optic was swapped during the maintenance window
```

### What the answer turn is served

Once the model has declared at least one standing, every later call is served the ledger as a system piece composed from the record: the context contract's `facts`, `limitations`, `evidenceRefs` and `nextSteps`, each bucket marked as declared by the model and quoting the declaration, then `noise` as a count and the results nobody named listed as undeclared — never as open. On the wire, and only on the wire, a tool result the model judged `noise` or `ruled-out` is replaced by a short ticket, `{ collapsed: true, standing, toolCallId }`, in place of its content. `open` and undeclared results are served in full, nothing is dropped or reordered, and `history` never changes, so the record still holds every result. `servedAt(snapshot, k)` rebuilds exactly what went out — the piece is the entry with `source: 'findings'` in `system.pieces` — and the receipt hashes it.

The `serve` option chooses how much of the pile stays beside the piece:

```ts
Agent.create({ provider, model })
  .tool(search)
  .findings({ serve: 'ledger-and-facts' }) // the default
  .build();
```

- `'ledger-and-facts'` (default): facts stay verbatim; noise and ruled-out results become tickets.
- `'ledger-only'`: fact results become tickets too and the model answers from the piece alone. This dial exists for the bench and is not a recommendation: it stays off by default until a run on a real model shows the answer does not drift when the same evidence arrives in a different order.

A second dial on the same door, `answerAsk`, appends a short ask to the end of the served piece under `'quote-facts'` — answer from the `facts` lines and copy each value as written, name an `evidenceRefs` or `nextSteps` result as unsettled, do not draw on a collapsed ticket, never invent a value — and is bench-gated the same way: the default is `'none'`, which serves the piece exactly as before and writes nothing new to the record, while `'quote-facts'` puts the run constant `findingsAnswerAsk` on the record so `servedAt` rebuilds the same bytes; it exists so `npm run bench:findings:shuffle`'s `ledger+ask` row can score the ask on a real model against the one-fact-in-twelve fidelity dip the design page measured.

### Held in the window — `keepLedgerFacts`

The piece restores a declared fact to the answer turn, but under a [window strategy](doc:window-strategies) the fact's *result* still left by recency: the refusal engine saw a result the model had declared a `fact` and one it had declared `noise` as the same bytes. Since 9.102.0 the window reads the ledger. A turn whose result the model declared a `fact` is held beyond `keepRecentTurns` — newest first, up to `keepLedgerFacts` turns — and the record names the hold with the refusal reason `ledger-fact`. Noise, ruled-out, open and undeclared turns leave oldest-first exactly as before, so "noise leaves first" is the same rule seen from the other side. The hold lives in the refusal engine, not in a strategy: `slidingWindow`, `tokenBudget`, `summarizeOldest` and a strategy you wrote all get it through `planRemoval`, and none of the three shipped strategies changed a byte.

```ts
Agent.create({ provider, model })
  .tool(search)
  .window(slidingWindow({ keepRecentTurns: 6 }))
  .findings({ keepLedgerFacts: 6 })   // default 4; `false` or 0 switches the hold off
  .build();
```

The same dial is `Agent.create({ keepLedgerFacts })`, beside `keepLastToolResults`; the `.findings()` door wins when both are given, a negative or non-integer value is refused at build, and without `.findings()` there is no ledger to hold from, so the option is accepted and does nothing. Four bounds compose, and none is optional:

- **By the model's claim only.** A turn is the removal unit, so its standing is its most valuable result's (`fact` over `open` over undeclared over `ruled-out` over `noise`): a parallel batch that answered one fact beside two noise results is one slot, and the noise stays with it. Nothing in the library reads a result's text to second-guess a standing; a result the model never named is undeclared and is not held.
- **The ceiling, spent newest first.** A held turn already inside `keepRecentTurns` costs nothing; the rest are admitted newest first up to the limit, and the ones turned away are counted as `yielded` on the record.
- **Anchored.** Nothing at or before the current request is pinnable, so a new user turn releases the whole previous loop.
- **The stand-down.** If the two previous visits both removed nothing and both named only pins (`last-tool-result` and/or `ledger-fact`), the fact pins release for one visit and the record says so. Both names count, because a turn held by both pins is reported under the recency pin's name — a fact stand-down reading only its own name would never see that turn blocking, and the two pins would take turns holding the window forever. A fact hold never exists without its ceiling and its stand-down.

Every visit's `WindowRecord` gains two optional keys, present only on an armed agent: `ledgerFacts` — what the hold kept (`pinned`: tool, turn, exact chars), how many turns the ceiling turned away (`yielded`), the `limit`, and `standDown: true` on the visit it released — and `droppedStandings`, the standing the model had declared for every tool result that left, by `toolCallId`, with `standing` absent for a result it never named. Both are filed by the stage, so a strategy you wrote carries them too, and an agent without `.findings()` files exactly the record it always did. The candidate a hold is built from is exported as `LedgerFactPin` — the tool-call ids a held turn carries, the tool it is named for, its turn and message index, and its exact chars — for a reader that wants to reason about what a visit could have held. What the model is *told* about a drop is unchanged: the notice names tools and counts, never a standing and never the model's own line.

Measured on `npm run bench:findings` (mock provider, 30 tool calls, a planted fact every third, a sliding window keeping 6 turns): the results of 2 of 10 planted facts reached the answer turn verbatim by recency alone, 6 under the default ceiling and 8 under a ceiling of 6, while the piece carried 9 of 10 on every armed row and the noise share of tool-result bytes on the wire stayed at the collapsed level; the design page has the print and its reading.

### A second source — `.findings({ judge })`

The ledger's standing is the model's claim, and the real-model runs measured how often that claim was right: about nineteen times in twenty on the stronger model, less on the weaker one. A calibrated classifier can read the same result and say what it is worth, with a probability per standing instead of a word. Pass one as `judge` and, after every tool result lands and before the next model call, the agent spends one classifier call on it and files the answer as a `JudgmentRow` beside the model's own `StandingRow`: the judge's `name` and the provider's `model` string, `against` — `proposition` when the call declared one, `question` when it did not — the chosen standing, the whole distribution in `probabilities`, `confidence`, `testsSubject` (the provider's probability that the result tests the subject at all), `usage`, `latencyMs`, and `clipped: true` when the result text was cut at 4000 characters before the judge saw it. The judge is asked what the *result* is to the declared proposition or the user's question — never why the model called the tool.

```ts
import { typesafe } from 'agentfootprint/classify';

const agent = Agent.create({ provider, model })
  .tool(search)
  .findings({ judge: typesafe() }) // TYPESAFE_API_KEY, or `typesafe({ apiKey })`
  .build();
```

Two sources are two rows, never one. The library does not merge the judge's reading with the model's, does not default a standing from a probability, and in this release serves nothing from a judgment: the answer turn still reads the model's own standing, and a result the model called `ruled-out` that the judge called `noise` stays on the record as exactly that disagreement. A failed call — a rate limit, an outage, an answer outside the four standings — is a `JudgmentErrorRow` with the provider's status and message and the run continues; a judge that is not a `Classifier` is refused at build. The events `agentfootprint.findings.judged` (standing, confidence, latency, tokens) and `agentfootprint.findings.judge_failed` carry identities, enums and numbers only; `agentfootprint.findings.standing` gains `agrees` — the model's standing against the judge's, present once a judgment exists for the result. Only a result the tool produced is judged: a denied, halted or declined call spends no classifier call. Without `judge`, nothing runs and an armed agent records the bytes it recorded before.

The classifier itself lives on `agentfootprint/classify`: the `Classifier` port (`name` plus `classify(request, signal?)`), the request and answer shapes — `ClassifyRequest`, `ClassifyQuestion` as `ClassifyChoiceQuestion`, `ClassifyNoulQuestion` or `ClassifyScoreQuestion`, `ClassifyResult`, `ClassifyAnswer` as `ClassifyChoiceAnswer`, `ClassifyNoulAnswer` or `ClassifyScoreAnswer` — and `ClassifierError` with its `status` and `retryable`. Two adapters ship: `typesafe(options)` (`TypesafeClassifierOptions`: `apiKey`, `model`, `baseUrl`, `timeout`, `maxRetries`, `retryDelayMs`) for TypeSafe's System One classifier, which retries 429 and 529 with exponential backoff and never puts the key in an error, and `mockClassifier(script)` (`MockClassifierScript`, a `MockClassifier` with every request on `calls`) for tests and the bench. The same port ranks a skill graph's entries: `classifierScorer(classifier)` on `agentfootprint/skill-graph` (options `ClassifierScorerOptions`) is an `EntryScorer` whose ranking *is* the provider's distribution — one choice question under the id `CLASSIFIER_SCORER_QUESTION`, the provider's pick as `chosen`, and on a provider failure the scorer name `CLASSIFIER_SCORER_UNAVAILABLE` with an empty ranking, so the cold-start entry pick takes over rather than a guess.

`npm run bench:findings:shuffle` measures it under `AF_SHUFFLE_JUDGE=mock|typesafe` — `judge-accuracy` against the planted truth, `judge-agrees` against the model's own standing, `judge-tokens` and `judge-latency-ms` read off the rows — and the design page (`docs/design/2026-09-findings-ledger.md` in the repository) names the serving policies the bench will decide between.

### Tool choice by classifier — `.toolChoice()`

The loop's most frequent choice is which tool, and the model makes it by generating a call — the record holds the call and nothing about the choice. `.toolChoice({ classifier })` asks the same classifier port a second reading of every one of those choices: at each model call the tools slot puts one `choice` question to it, under the fixed id `TOOL_CHOICE_QUESTION`, whose criteria are the tools about to be served — the merged wire minus the always-served doors, each by its own description — over a state of the user's message and the active skill id. The answer lands on `AgentState.toolChoices` as a `ToolChoiceRow` *before* the call: `offered`, `ranked` (a `ToolChoiceScore` per name the provider scored, highest first, an unscored tool absent rather than zero), `chosen` (the provider's own pick, absent when it named nothing offered), `confidence`, `usage`, `latencyMs`, and `served` with `narrowed`. After the reply the call-llm stage files a `ToolChoiceOutcomeRow`: `called` (the model's tool calls in order, empty on an answer), `firstAgrees` (whether the first call is the pick, absent when either side is absent) and any `miss`. A failed classifier call is a `ToolChoiceErrorRow` with the provider's status and message, and the full set is served. The three row kinds are `ToolChoiceEntry`; the key is a `ToolChoiceLedger` — flat, append-only, a fresh array per write.

```ts
import { typesafe } from 'agentfootprint/classify';

const agent = Agent.create({ provider, model })
  .tool(lookupOrder)
  .tool(refundCharge)
  .tool(listInvoices)
  .toolChoice({ classifier: typesafe(), serve: { top: 2 } })
  .build();
await agent.run({ message: 'refund order 42' });
agent.getSnapshot()?.sharedState.toolChoices; // pick → served → called, per call
```

The model's call is never overridden and, by default (`serve: 'all'`), nothing is served differently: an advisory agent's requests are byte for byte the unarmed agent's, and the record gains the rows and nothing else. `serve: { top: N }` is the narrowing dial: the tools slot commits the classifier's top-N plus the doors as the served list, at the one site where the served list is built, so the request, the receipt's `tools.schemaHashes` and `servedAt(k).tools.schemas` all name the narrowed list by construction. The doors are never narrowed away and never offered as candidates: `read_skill`, `list_skills`, `skip_step` and `present` — the constant `ALWAYS_SERVED_TOOLS` — plus every name in `alwaysServe`. The full wire is served, with the reason on the row as a `NarrowSkipReason`, when the classifier failed or scored fewer than N names (`unavailable`), fewer than N + 1 candidates were offered (`too-few`), the previous call's outcome carried a miss (`after-miss`), or the call is the out-of-budget wrap-up (`wrap-up`). A miss is a fact, not a refusal: when a narrowed call's reply names a tool outside `served`, the outcome row carries `miss.wanted`, the dispatcher answers the call exactly as it answered an off-wire call before (`agentfootprint.tools.answered_off_wire`), and the next call serves the full wire. `reactMode: 'classic'` is refused at build, as it is for `.findings()`.

The events carry identities, enums and numbers only: `agentfootprint.tool_choice.picked` (the pick, its confidence, how many tools were offered and served, whether the list was narrowed and why not, latency and tokens), `agentfootprint.tool_choice.outcome` (`called`, `firstAgrees`, `missed`) and `agentfootprint.tool_choice.failed` (status, latency) — never a description, never the message. `npm run bench:tool-choice` measures both dials on the mock provider from the record alone — `first-agrees`, `misses`, `extra-calls`, `tools-slot-bytes` from the receipt's `requestMeasurement`, `pick-tokens`, `pick-latency-ms` — and exits non-zero if an unarmed twin's tools-slot bytes move; the design page (`docs/design/2026-09-scored-choice.md` in the repository, step 4) has the print and its reading, and names what the state does not yet carry (the conversation so far).

## Composition with other Agents

An Agent is a runner, just like LLMCall, Sequence, Parallel, Conditional. Use them as steps in larger graphs:

```ts
import { Sequence } from 'agentfootprint';

const research = Sequence.create()
  .step('plan', plannerLLM)
  .step('execute', researchAgent)
  .step('summarize', summarizerLLM)
  .build();
```

There is no separate "multi-agent" class — agents *are* the building blocks. See [Patterns](doc:key-concepts#patterns--named-compositions) for Reflexion / ToT / Debate / Map-Reduce / Swarm recipes.

## Anti-patterns

- Don't subclass Agent for a "smarter" agent — use `.skill()` / `.instruction()` to inject behavior. Subclassing breaks composition.
- Don't put async I/O in tool `execute`'s synchronous setup — it runs every iteration. Cache outside; pure dispatch inside.
- Don't bypass `maxIterations` to "let the agent decide" — every loop has a cost ceiling. Set it explicitly; observe `agentfootprint.agent.iteration_end` to track.
